proof:
# Attained critical-cap selection by convex reciprocal exit cost
over the whole available critical-cap menu, rather than an arbitrarily
chosen large integer tilt. It gives an attained cap, exact first-exit
optimality, and preservation of specified one-cap residual KKT data.
It does not give a numerical overshoot bound in terms of the OC budget.

The convex reciprocal-exit invariant in Section3 was independently
suggested by root. The projected-menu closure, attainment, and KKT
preservation below give its exact finite interface.

## 1. Fixed data and the full critical menu

Work in the positive d-volume setting, d>=1. Let C be an actual convex
body, let P be its finite set of positive d-volume integer bases, and let
mu be the sum of those section volumes. Fix a nonzero continuous normal
u, an integer source base p in P, and a real source threshold c such that

    m(p):=min_(x in C_p) u.x < c.                       (1)

Thus the strict residual at p has positive d-volume. The variable caps
are the actual ambient halfspaces

    H_a={ (z,x): u.x+a.(z-p)>=c },      a in R^n.        (2)

Let Q>0 be the attained global raw mixed depth. Let A be a specified
closed polyhedron of integer-normal parameters. For this critical-cap
version, it MUST include an equation ensuring that H_a passes through
at least one fixed deepest point. For a prescribed deepest point
(z_*,x_*), impose

    a.(z_*-p)=c-u.x_*.

Several such anchor equations may be imposed at once. Apart from this
required anchor, any further closed polyhedral constraints are allowed.
Additional
polyhedral constraints will preserve residual KKT data in Section7.
Assume the critical menu

    M={a in A: mu(H_a)=Q}                              (3)

is nonempty. Every member is then genuinely minimizing at each of its
prescribed deepest anchors. No statement is inferred from a cap that
merely has a convenient local section size.

Fix distinct row destinations z_1,...,z_N in P and positive weights
theta_j with sum theta_j=1 and sum theta_j z_j=p. Write

    B=conv{z_1,...,z_N},
    E=span{z_j-p},       d_j=z_j-p.

Then p lies in relint B. The dimension-zero case is immediate: all
destinations equal p, there is no exit, and any member of M suffices.
Henceforth assume dim E>=1.

## 2. Closedness of the projected critical menu

The set

    S={proj_E a:a in M} subset E                       (4)

is closed, despite possible unbounded components of a perpendicular
to E. The conclusion is particular to the finite cap-mass structure;
it is not the false general claim that projections of closed sets are
always closed.

To prove it, take a_l in M with proj_E a_l converging to b. Passing to
a subsequence, every one of the finitely many numbers

    a_l.(z-p),       z in P,

has a limit in the compact extended line [-infinity,infinity]. Let I
be the indices with finite limits v_z and let I_+,I_- be the other
two sets. Choose L so large that a margin coefficient at least L
captures its entire fiber strictly and one at most -L excludes its
entire fiber strictly; this is possible because all fibers are bounded.

The set of a in A satisfying

    a.(z-p)>=L on I_+,       a.(z-p)<=-L on I_-

is a closed polyhedron. Its image under the linear map

    a -> (proj_E a, (a.(z-p))_(z in I))

is a closed polyhedron, by finite elimination of variables. It contains
the corresponding image of every sufficiently late a_l, so it contains
the limit (b,(v_z)_(z in I)). Choose a finite parameter a realizing
that limit image and those saturation inequalities.

On each finite-limit fiber its cap mass equals the limiting cap mass,
by ordinary continuous cap-tail continuity for the fixed nonzero u.
On each infinite-limit fiber it realizes exactly the limiting full or
empty trace. Thus mu(H_a)=lim_l mu(H_(a_l))=Q. It belongs to A and
projects to b, proving (4) closed.

This proof also explains why imposing any further fixed closed
polyhedral normal constraints does not invalidate the selection.

## 3. Convexity of the reciprocal first-exit cost

For z in B define m(z)=min_(x in C_z)u.x. This function is finite and
convex: combine minimizing section points to obtain its convexity
inequality. It is lower semicontinuous by compactness of C. Along each
closed segment [p,z_j] it is continuous. At an endpoint this follows
by combining its minimizing point with the opposite endpoint section
for the upper bound, and compactness for the lower bound. Interior
continuity follows from finite convexity on an interval.

For b in E define the compact residual projection

    K_b={z in B: m(z)+b.(z-p)<=c}.                      (5)

It is the projection of the compact convex set
{(z,x) in C:z in B, u.x+b.(z-p)<=c}. It contains a relative
neighborhood of p by (1). One direct verification chooses a point
x_p in C_p with u.x_p<c and arbitrary points in the finitely many
destination sections, then takes sufficiently small convex
combinations with (p,x_p).

Let t_j(b) be the largest t in [0,1] for which p+t d_j belongs to K_b.
Thus 0<t_j<=1. The source inequality is strict, so a positive interval
always belongs to K_b. The set along the segment is an interval by
convexity. This is the first-exit fraction used by the stopped-row
construction; when no exit occurs before the endpoint, its value is 1.

Put delta=c-m(p)>0. For s>=1 set

    h_j(s)=s[c-m(p+d_j/s)].                            (6)

The function h_j is continuous and concave: s m(p+d_j/s) is the
perspective of the convex function m, restricted to this ray. More
explicitly, that perspective convexity follows directly by expressing
the point at a convex combination of two positive s values as the
corresponding denominator-weighted convex combination of the two base
points and applying convexity of m.

For s_2>s_1>=1, convexity also gives

    m(p+d_j/s_2)
      <= (s_1/s_2)m(p+d_j/s_1)+(1-s_1/s_2)m(p),

and hence

    h_j(s_2)>=h_j(s_1)+delta(s_2-s_1).                 (7)

Therefore h_j is strictly increasing, tends to infinity, and its inverse
above h_j(1) is Lipschitz with constant at most 1/delta.

Writing x=b.d_j, the exact reciprocal exit is

    s_j(b):=1/t_j(b)
       =1                         if x<=h_j(1),
       =h_j^(-1)(x)               if x>h_j(1).         (8)

Indeed p+d_j/s belongs to K_b exactly when x<=h_j(s), and the largest
admissible t is the smallest admissible s. The epigraph of s_j is

    { (b,s): s>=1, b.d_j<=h_j(s) },                    (9)

which is convex because h_j is concave. Thus s_j is a finite continuous
convex function on E. In particular the total reciprocal exit cost

    C(b)=sum_j theta_j s_j(b)                          (10)

is finite, continuous and convex. It is exactly the correction factor
in the barycentric first-exit reweighting, not an approximation to it.

## 4. Coercivity, attained selection, and inclusion maximality

The cost C is coercive on E. Since the d_j span E and have a positive
weighted mean zero, every nonzero b in E has max_j b.d_j>0. Compactness
of the unit sphere in E therefore gives eta>0 such that

    max_j b.d_j>=eta |b|.                              (11)

Let L=c-min_{(z,x) in C,z in B} u.x>0. Formula (6) gives h_j(s)<=Ls,
so (8) gives s_j(b)>=(b.d_j)/L whenever that numerator is positive.
Consequently

    C(b)>=(min_j theta_j) eta |b|/L -> infinity.        (12)

By Section2 the nonempty menu S is closed. The continuous coercive
cost therefore attains its minimum on S, and its minimizing set is
compact. This does not assert S is convex, that the minimizer is unique,
or that the minimizer set is convex.

The sets K_b vary continuously in Hausdorff distance with b. Upper
continuity follows from compactness. For lower continuity, take a
feasible pair (z,x) at b and mix it with the fixed strictly feasible
(p,x_p). The new pair has strict margin and belongs to the retained
set for every sufficiently close b'. Letting the mixing coefficient
tend to zero approximates z. Compactness converts this pointwise
approximation into Hausdorff convergence. Every K_b is full-dimensional
in E, so its E-dimensional volume is continuous under this convergence.

Among the compact set of C-minimizers choose one b_* maximizing
vol_E(K_b). Lift it to some a_* in M using the definition of S. This
is one finite, actually critical cap. It has both properties:

* There is no other member of the same constrained critical menu with
  every listed exit fraction at least t_j(b_*) and one strictly larger.
  Such a member would strictly decrease (10), since every theta_j>0.
* Its residual projection on the ENTIRE row hull is inclusion-maximal:
  no other member has K_(b_*) properly contained in K_b. Inclusion makes
  all listed exit fractions larger or equal, so that member would also
  minimize C. Proper inclusion of full-dimensional compact convex sets
  strictly increases E-volume, contradicting the secondary choice.

These are Pareto and inclusion maximality statements, not a claim that
one critical cap simultaneously dominates every other critical cap.
If a deterministic tie convention is desired, fix coordinates in E and
successively minimize them over the compact secondary maximizing set.
For the chosen projection, choose a minimum-Euclidean-norm lift in its
nonempty closed critical fiber and break remaining ties in the same way.
All these finite choices are attained.

## 5. Exact first-order conditions and the polytopal formula

The scalar function in (8) has an explicit convex subdifferential. Above
h_j(1), writing s=h_j^(-1)(x)>1, it is the interval

    [1/h'_(j,-)(s), 1/h'_(j,+)(s)].                    (13)

Both one-sided slopes of h_j are positive and at least delta by (7).
Below h_j(1) the subdifferential is {0}; at that value it is
[0,1/h'_(j,+)(1)], with 1/infinity interpreted as zero if needed.
Thus

    partial C(b)=sum_j theta_j (partial s_j(b.d_j)) d_j. (14)

For every differentiable one-sided feasible curve in S with
b(epsilon)=b_*+epsilon v+o(epsilon), minimality gives the exact necessary
condition

    max_{g in partial C(b_*)} g.v >=0.                 (15)

The derivative exists because a finite convex function has the stated
directional derivative, and here the local Lipschitz property controls
the o(epsilon) error. No convexity of the critical menu is assumed. If
one restricts to a convex feasible subset of S, the usual subgradient
normal-cone condition for that convex minimization is available; it is
not asserted for an arbitrary nonconvex menu.

When the actual restricted body is polytopal, write its convex
piecewise-affine one-dimensional profile as

    m(p+t d_j)=max_l(alpha_(jl)+beta_(jl)t),  0<=t<=1.

Every alpha_(jl)<=m(p)<c. Equations (6)--(9) become the finite exact
formula

    s_j(b)=max{1, max_l [(b.d_j+beta_(jl))/(c-alpha_(jl))]}.
                                                               (16)

Thus C is convex piecewise affine. Its subdifferential is the weighted
sum of convex hulls of the active affine slopes in (16); this gives a
finite exact first-order certificate on every specified feasible cell.
There is no assumption that the full critical menu itself is polyhedral.

## 6. What has and has not been optimized

This selection removes avoidable large normal components in the exact
cost relevant to the stopped row. In the previously audited A,T,T
example, arbitrary isolating tilts made C diverge while Q stayed fixed;
the present theorem instead selects a finite minimum of C over the
whole constrained critical menu.

It proves neither C(b_*)=1 nor a bound on C(b_*) in terms only of d,
the occupied parity count, or Q/M. The compactness constants in
(11)--(12) depend on the actual row and body. Such a numerical bound
would be a genuinely additional theorem, not a consequence of
attainment or convexity of the scalar objective.

## 7. Preserving the original one-cap residual optimizer and KKT row

The closed polyhedron A in Section1 can enforce preservation of a given
optimal one-cap residual program. Let one original cap be replaced by
H_a while all others remain fixed. At a base z write

    f_z(a)=|C_z intersect H_a^c|^(1/d),
    ebar_z=min_(other caps H) |C_z intersect H^c|^(1/d),

with ebar_z=infinity if there are no other caps. Suppose h,g,lambda,mu
are the original optimal primal values, slopes and KKT multipliers.
The new obstacle is min(ebar_z,f_z(a)). Impose the following rules:

* If lambda_z>0, require f_z(a)>=h_z. If additionally ebar_z>h_z,
  require f_z(a)<=h_z as well.
* If lambda_z=0 and ebar_z>h_z, require f_z(a)<=h_z.
* In all other cases impose no further condition at that base.

At a positive-lambda base the old obstacle equaled h_z, so necessarily
ebar_z>=h_z. The first rule makes the new obstacle exactly h_z. At
every zero-lambda base the remaining rule makes the new obstacle at
most h_z. Thus h remains primal feasible and all obstacle
complementary-slackness equations remain valid. The slope constraints,
their multipliers, and the stationarity equations do not change.
Consequently the SAME primal optimizer and KKT multipliers remain
optimal for the modified cap family. Its explicit martingale coupling
can be retained without recomputation.

These rules define a closed polyhedron in a. For fixed u the function
f_z(a) is a continuous nonincreasing function of the single affine
parameter a.(z-p). Its levels strictly between zero and V_z^(1/d)
have unique ordinary section quantiles; its endpoint level sets are
also closed half-lines, with the appropriate whole/empty alternatives.
Therefore each displayed inequality is a linear halfspace constraint
on a, or is automatic. The old parameter satisfies every rule, so
these extra constraints do not destroy nonemptiness. Fixing the source
trace by (2) also keeps the selected residual cap active there whenever
it was active originally.

This is a t=1 program-preservation statement. It is not an unproved
extension to arbitrary unions of several varying caps. Nor does
primal feasibility alone ensure that the entire original cap family
still covers the mixed set; that separate requirement is treated next.

## 8. Preserving coverage by fixed deepest-face circuits

Suppose the selected caps belong to one of the proved fixed witness
circuits at a deepest point (z_*,x_*), with positive coefficients rho_i
and unchanged continuous normals satisfying sum rho_i u_i=0. Keep
each modified cap globally critical and passing through that same
point, as required by the linear anchor equations in A.

Every such cap has nonpositive margin at every deepest point. If a
deepest point had a strictly positive margin, raising the threshold
slightly would retain it and remove a positive slab from the original
proper anchor section, contradicting its depth Q. Thus the weighted
sum of the new cap margins is nonpositive at all deepest bases and
zero at its witness. It is a pure affine function of the integer
base because the continuous normals still positively balance.

Its zero face contains the witness's minimal face in the convex hull
of all deepest bases. On every real base in that face, the weighted
cap-margin sum is zero for every continuous point. At least one of
the closed caps therefore contains that point, so the modified
circuit still covers the whole continuous plane above that face.
This is exactly the already proved fixed-face witness mechanism,
applied to the newly selected genuinely critical caps.

Retain all original slack circuits for nondeepest bases. Then selecting
critical caps through the same fixed witness points with the same
continuous normals preserves the actual positive-fiber cover. If a
cap is shared by several original witness circuits, impose all its
original anchor equations; they are compatible because the old cap
satisfies them. Any separately required zero-measure-fiber covering
caps are likewise retained.

Coverage in this application follows from these circuit and anchor
conditions, not merely from the KKT feasibility rules of Section7.
Neither this coverage fact nor the attained exit optimization yet
converts the stopped-flow correction into the numerical OC bound.
